name: Badarian Culture
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: The earliest well-defined farming culture of Upper Egypt, and the first casualty of the 2013 radiocarbon model.

name: El-Omari
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: A Lower Egyptian Neolithic settlement near Helwan, plainer in its material culture than its Upper Egyptian contemporaries.

name: Hierakonpolis
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: An Upper Egyptian power centre with monumental elite tombs, industrial-scale brewing, and buried elephants.

name: Maadi-Buto Culture
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: The last independent culture of Lower Egypt, absorbed into the expanding Naqada world well before any king unified anything.

name: Merimde Beni Salama
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: One of the largest Neolithic settlements of the Delta, and a site whose published dates disagree by five hundred years.

name: Naqada I
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: The first phase of the Naqada sequence: black-topped pottery, white cross-lined ware, and the beginnings of a distinctly Upper Egyptian world.

name: Naqada II
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: Trade networks widen, burials grow unequal, and Upper Egyptian material culture starts moving north into the Delta.

name: Naqada III
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: State formation proper: walled towns, royal-scale tombs, the first writing, and the kings who came before the First Dynasty.

name: Tomb U-j at Abydos
under: Predynastic Egypt < Ancient Egypt < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: The richest tomb at Abydos before the First Dynasty, holding the earliest known Egyptian writing.

name: Kerma Phase
under: Kingdom of Kush < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa

name: Meroitic Phase
under: Kingdom of Kush < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa
summary: Meroë as capital; Meroitic script still undeciphered.

name: Napatan Phase
under: Kingdom of Kush < Nile Valley & Northeast Africa < Africa

name: Apollo 11 Cave
summary: Namibian shelter holding seven painted stone plaques, four figurative, among the oldest known figurative art in Africa.

name: Bantu Homeland Phase
summary: The long local development of proto-Bantu in the Cameroon Grassfields, before any outward expansion across the continent.

name: Blombos Cave
summary: A South African cave holding engraved ochre, shell beads and the oldest known drawing.

name: Bodo
summary: Middle Awash cranium anchoring the mid-Pleistocene African record, bearing cut marks suggestive of deliberate defleshing.

name: Border Cave
summary: A South African site whose sequence runs from the Middle Stone Age into the present, including the earliest Later Stone Age toolkit.

name: Capsian Culture
summary: Epipalaeolithic to early Neolithic tradition of the eastern Maghreb, known for its shell-and-ash mound sites and later pressure-flaked bladelets.

name: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
summary: Western Cape shelter whose engraved ostrich eggshell containers are among the earliest deliberately produced graphic marks known.

name: Enkapune Ya Muto
summary: Kenyan rock shelter with a claim to the earliest Later Stone Age blade technology in Africa, and the oldest directly dated ornaments anywhere.

name: Fayum Neolithic
summary: One of the earliest well-documented farming and herding sequences in the Nile Valley, following the Qarunian foragers of the same oasis.

name: Gobero
summary: The largest and oldest known Stone Age cemetery in the Sahara, preserving two distinct Holocene populations either side of a drought.

name: Gona
summary: Afar locality holding some of the oldest securely dated Oldowan stone tools, anchoring the industry's 2.6 Ma start.

name: Green Sahara
summary: The window when the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grassland, and people lived across what is now the largest hot desert on Earth.

name: Hadar
summary: The Afar site that produced AL 288-1, 'Lucy', the Australopithecus afarensis skeleton that made early bipedalism concrete.

name: Herto
summary: Middle Awash locality that produced Homo sapiens idaltu, among the oldest near-modern human fossils.

name: Ishango
summary: A Semliki River site in the DRC, famous for a notched bone sometimes read as an early tally device, and unusually hard to date.

name: Jebel Irhoud
summary: Moroccan site holding the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens fossils, which moved the species' origin back by roughly 100,000 years.

name: Kabwe
summary: Zambian cranium once called Homo rhodesiensis, and the clearest case in African palaeoanthropology of a textbook number being wrong by 200,000 years.

name: Khartoum Mesolithic
summary: Pottery-using but pre-agricultural hunter-fisher-gatherers of the central Nile, known for wavy-line and dotted-wavy-line ceramics.

name: Klasies River Mouth
summary: A South African cave sequence with some of the earliest anatomically modern human remains outside East Africa.

name: Laetoli
summary: Tanzanian site preserving the oldest confirmed hominin footprints, showing upright walking 350,000 years before the first stone tools.

name: Melka Kunture
summary: A high-altitude Ethiopian sequence running from Oldowan to Middle Stone Age, and the site of a live dispute over the world's earliest Acheulean.

name: Nabta Playa
summary: A seasonal lake basin in the Egyptian Sahara with cattle burials and a megalithic circle, occupied while the desert was green.

name: Nok Culture
summary: Central Nigerian culture producing sub-Saharan Africa's earliest large-scale sculptural tradition, and some of its earliest iron smelting.

name: Olduvai Gorge
summary: A Tanzanian ravine cutting through two million years of deposits, the site that made early human archaeology a dated science.

name: Olorgesailie
summary: A Kenyan rift basin recording the Acheulean-to-Middle Stone Age transition, tied to Middle Pleistocene environmental instability.

name: Omo Kibish
summary: The Ethiopian site of Omo I, for decades the oldest known fossil of our own species.

name: Pinnacle Point
summary: Southern Cape caves with early evidence for marine resource use, heat treatment of stone and pigment, and one of the most precisely dated MSA sequences.

name: Rising Star Cave
summary: The Dinaledi Chamber, source of the Homo naledi fossils, whose surprisingly young age placed a small-brained hominin alongside early Homo sapiens.

name: Sibudu Cave
summary: KwaZulu-Natal shelter with the finest-resolution Middle Stone Age sequence in southern Africa, from pre-Still Bay through Howiesons Poort to the final MSA.

name: Sterkfontein
summary: Cradle of Humankind cave system holding 'Mrs Ples' and 'Little Foot', and the most actively contested chronology in African palaeoanthropology.

name: Swartkrans
summary: Cradle of Humankind cave with the earliest well-dated Paranthropus robustus and among the oldest Oldowan tools in southern Africa.

name: Taforalt
summary: The most extensively radiocarbon-dated Later Stone Age site in North Africa, and the location of the continent's oldest known cemetery.

name: Turkana Basin
summary: The most continuous tuff-dated hominin sequence in East Africa, spanning Koobi Fora, Nariokotome and Kokiselei on both shores of Lake Turkana.

name: Wadi Kubbaniya
summary: Late Palaeolithic sites near Aswan, once thought to hold the world's earliest cereal cultivation, and a cautionary case in contamination.

name: Machu Picchu
summary: A royal estate on the Vilcabamba ridge, built under Pachacuti and abandoned within a century of Spanish arrival.

name: Qhapaq Ñan
summary: The Andean road network that made the empire governable, running some 30,000 kilometres across six modern countries.

name: Classic Maya
summary: Classic Maya florescence of city-states and hieroglyphic writing.

name: Tikal
under: Classic Maya < Maya Civilization < Mesoamerica < Americas
summary: The largest excavated Classic Maya city, and the clearest single illustration that the Maya were never one empire.

name: Monte Albán
summary: The Zapotec capital on a levelled mountaintop above the Oaxaca valley.

name: Chaco Canyon
summary: The administrative and ceremonial centre of the Ancestral Puebloan world, linked by engineered roads across the San Juan Basin.

name: Cahokia
summary: The largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, and the reason 'Mississippian' names a civilization rather than a pottery style.

name: Civil War & Reconstruction
summary: Union defeated the Confederacy; ended slavery and reshaped the American republic.

name: Archaic Period
summary: A long, regionally varied North American period of adapting to post-ice-age environments, broad diets, and later early farming.

name: Bering Land Bridge
summary: The dry land connection that intermittently linked Siberia and Alaska during the last ice age.

name: Caballo Muerto
summary: A complex of monumental adobe platforms in the Moche valley, with friezes predating the Moche state by a thousand years.

name: Cactus Hill
summary: A Virginia sand-dune site with a possible stone-tool layer below a Clovis level.

name: Cerro Sechin
summary: A Peruvian site famous for granite friezes of dismembered warriors, and for a widely repeated early date that its own excavation report does not support.

name: Chinchorro Culture
summary: Coastal foragers of the Atacama who deliberately mummified their dead — including children and the stillborn — for four thousand years.

name: Clovis Culture
summary: A short-lived North American tradition of distinctive fluted stone points.

name: Cooper's Ferry
summary: An Idaho site occupied before the ice-free corridor was passable, which is the argument for a Pacific coastal route.

name: Folsom Culture
summary: A bison-hunting tradition that followed Clovis across much of the North American plains.

name: Huaca Prieta
summary: A Peruvian coastal mound with 13,000 years of human presence, cotton by 6,800 years ago, and mound-building sustained for three and a half millennia.

name: Las Vegas Culture
summary: The oldest known archaeological complex on the Ecuadorian coast, with squash and bottle gourd cultivated by 9,000 years ago.

name: Old Copper Complex
summary: Great Lakes peoples working native copper into tools and points — among the oldest metalworking traditions anywhere on Earth.

name: Paisley Caves
summary: Oregon caves with early human coprolites, basketry, and a Western Stemmed stone-point tradition.

name: Paleoindian Period
summary: A broad North American label for the earliest widespread post-ice-age traditions, including Clovis and Folsom.

name: Poverty Point
summary: Concentric earthen ridges and mounds in Louisiana, built by a hunter-fisher-gatherer society with a continental trade reach.

name: Pre-Clovis Horizon
summary: The broad label for accepted American sites older than the Clovis tool tradition.

name: Taperinha
summary: An Amazonian shell midden holding the oldest pottery in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Valdivia Culture
summary: An early ceramic culture of coastal Ecuador, long claimed as the oldest pottery in the Americas — which it is not.

name: Watson Brake
summary: Eleven earthen mounds in Louisiana raised by hunter-gatherers, nineteen centuries before Poverty Point.

name: Western Stemmed Tradition
summary: A stone-point tradition of the American Far West that runs alongside Clovis without descending from it.

name: White Sands Footprints
summary: Human footprints in New Mexico that may date to the height of the last ice age.

name: Ilkhanate
under: Mongol Empire < Central Asia & the Steppe

name: Afanasievo Culture
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: An early pastoral culture of the Altai and Minusinsk Basin with strong ties to western steppe populations.

name: Altyn-Depe
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A walled town of the Namazga culture with a stepped tower, craft quarters and trade reaching Mundigak and Shahr-i Sokhta.

name: Anau
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: The Kopet Dag tell that names the Anau horizon, spanning the Chalcolithic in its north mound and the Bronze Age in its south.

name: Andronovo Culture
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A Bronze Age network of steppe communities extending across Kazakhstan and southern Siberia.

name: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: An oasis-based Bronze Age culture of Central Asia known for planned settlements, irrigation, and long-distance exchange.

name: Gonur Depe
under: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex < Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: The principal city of the Oxus civilisation in the Murghab delta, with palace, temple and monumental enclosure.

name: Botai Culture
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A northern Kazakh settlement tradition famous for early intensive use of horses.

name: Denisova Cave
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A Siberian cave with a long record of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans.

name: Jeitun Culture
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: The earliest farming in Central Asia: mudbrick villages in the Kopet Dag piedmont, with barley, einkorn, sheep and goat.

name: Kelteminar Culture
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: Hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Aral basin and the Amu Darya delta, in contact with the farming villages to their south.

name: Begash
under: Inner Asian Mountain Corridor < Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A Dzhungar Mountains campsite holding the earliest directly dated broomcorn millet outside China, together with wheat, in a cremation burial.

name: Tasbas
under: Inner Asian Mountain Corridor < Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A high-altitude Kazakh site where mobile pastoralists were threshing their own wheat, barley, millet and peas by the late second millennium.

name: Sarazm
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A Chalcolithic town in the Zeravshan valley of Tajikistan, smelting copper and trading lapis and turquoise between the steppe, Mesopotamia and the Indus.

name: Seima-Turbino Phenomenon
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: A distinctive kit of cast-bronze weapons that appears across five thousand kilometres of Eurasia without an accompanying culture, pottery or burial rite.

name: Tarim Basin Mummies
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: Naturally desiccated burials in the Taklamakan, long read as evidence of a western migration into China, and genomically nothing of the kind.

name: Yamnaya Horizon
under: Central Asian Prehistory < Central Asia & the Steppe
summary: Mobile pastoral communities of the Pontic-Caspian steppe whose movements had major effects across Europe and Asia.

name: Tianyuan Cave
under: Late Pleistocene China < China < East Asia
summary: A femur near Beijing from one of the earliest directly dated modern humans in East Asia.

name: Xianrendong Cave
under: Late Pleistocene China < China < East Asia
summary: A Jiangxi cave holding what may be the oldest pottery in the world, made by foragers during the Last Glacial Maximum — if the dates hold.

name: Yuchanyan Cave
under: Late Pleistocene China < China < East Asia
summary: A Hunan cave with early pottery and wild rice, dated by a study designed specifically to get the chronology right.

name: Erlitou
summary: A large early Bronze Age centre in Henan with palace foundations and bronze workshops, and the site the entire Xia argument is actually about.

name: Cishan Culture
summary: A north China millet culture whose storage pits produced the claim that cereal farming here began at the Pleistocene boundary.

name: Dawenkou Culture
summary: An eastern China culture of elaborate burials and incised pottery marks sometimes discussed, carefully, in relation to later Chinese writing.

name: Daxi Culture
summary: A middle Yangtze culture with some of the earliest walled settlements in China, at Chengtoushan.

name: Hemudu Culture
summary: A waterlogged lower Yangtze site that preserved wooden mortise-and-tenon architecture and some of the earliest cultivated rice.

name: Hongshan Culture
summary: A jade-working and temple-building culture of the West Liao River region in northeast China.

name: Jiahu
summary: An early Henan village known for rice, bone flutes, and much-debated incised marks.

name: Liangzhu Culture
summary: A Yangtze-delta society with a walled centre, jade traditions, and major dams and waterways.

name: The Liangzhu Hydraulic System
under: Liangzhu Culture < Chinese Neolithic < China < East Asia
summary: Eleven dams and levees around the Liangzhu city, the earliest large-scale water management known anywhere.

name: Longshan Culture
summary: A late Neolithic tradition of black pottery, walled settlements, and regional change in the Yellow River basin.

name: Peiligang Culture
summary: An early farming culture of the central Henan plain, associated with millet cultivation and small villages.

name: Qijia Culture
summary: A northwest culture straddling the Neolithic and Bronze Age, central to arguments about how metallurgy reached China.

name: Shijiahe Culture
summary: A middle Yangtze late Neolithic culture of walled settlements and rice, contemporary with Longshan further north.

name: Xinglongwa Culture
summary: A northeast China culture of planned villages, jade working, and the earliest millet grains anywhere to be dated directly rather than by context.

name: Yangshao Culture
summary: A major painted-pottery farming tradition of the middle Yellow River valley.

name: Spring and Autumn Period
under: Eastern Zhou < Zhou Dynasty < China < East Asia
summary: Time of Confucius and Laozi.

name: Warring States Period
under: Eastern Zhou < Zhou Dynasty < China < East Asia
summary: Seven kingdoms fought for supremacy; Hundred Schools of Thought.

name: Early Jōmon
summary: A Jōmon stage of growing regional diversity in settlements and pottery styles.

name: Final Jōmon
summary: The final Jōmon stage, ending at different times in different parts of Japan.

name: Incipient Jōmon
summary: The earliest Jōmon stage, marked by some of the world's oldest securely dated pottery.

name: Initial Jōmon
summary: A long early Jōmon stage when pottery traditions diversified across the Japanese islands.

name: The Late Jomon Population Decline
summary: A sustained demographic contraction across the Japanese archipelago, centuries before wet rice arrived.

name: Late Jōmon
summary: A later Jōmon stage before the regionally staggered transition to Yayoi farming communities.

name: Middle Jōmon
summary: A Jōmon stage known for large settlements and elaborate pottery in several regions.

name: Sannai Maruyama
summary: A large, long-lived Jomon settlement with monumental timber posts and long-distance exchange, built by people who were not farmers.

name: Heisei
summary: Emperor Akihito. Ended by voluntary abdication.

name: Meiji
summary: Meiji Restoration and rapid modernization. Emperor Meiji (Mutsuhito).

name: Reiwa
summary: Current era. Emperor Naruhito.

name: Shōwa
summary: Longest modern era. Emperor Shōwa (Hirohito). Spans militarism, WWII, and postwar boom.

name: Taishō
summary: Democratic reform era; Emperor Taishō (Yoshihito).

name: Arrival of Millet in Korea
summary: Foxtail and broomcorn millet reach the peninsula from northeast China, Korea's first cultivated cereals and some two millennia before rice.

name: Arrival of Rice in Korea
summary: Paddy rice reaches Korea by a Shandong-Liaodong route, the agricultural change that would shortly cross to Japan and begin the Yayoi.

name: Habsburg Era
under: Holy Roman Empire < Central Europe < Europe
summary: Habsburg dynasty held the Holy Roman Emperor title almost continuously from 1438 to 1806.

name: Archaic Greece
summary: Formative period of the polis, colonization, and archaic art.

name: Greek Dark Ages
summary: The centuries between the collapse of Mycenaean palace society and the emergence of the city-states: writing was lost and populations fell, but iron came into use and the epics took shape.

name: Minoan Civilization
summary: Bronze Age Cretan civilization; palace at Knossos.

name: Mycenaean Civilization
summary: Late Bronze Age Greek civilization; the world of Homer's epics.

name: Crisis of the Third Century
under: Roman Empire < Ancient Rome < Mediterranean < Europe
summary: Fifty years of civil war, plague, and near-collapse.

name: Altamira Cave Art
summary: People added painted and engraved images to Altamira in northern Spain over a very long span.

name: Azilian
summary: The first post-glacial culture of southwest France and northern Spain, with flat harpoons and painted pebbles.

name: Bell Beaker Culture
summary: Bell-shaped drinking vessels, new burial customs, and large population movements reshaped much of western Europe.

name: Cardial and Impressed Ware
summary: The Mediterranean route: farming carried west by sea along the northern Mediterranean coast, from Liguria to Portugal.

name: Chauvet Cave Art
summary: Artists made charcoal drawings in this French cave during two Upper Paleolithic visits.

name: Corded Ware Culture
summary: A wide European culture known for cord-marked pots and single graves spread from the Rhine to the Baltic.

name: Cucuteni-Trypillia
summary: The great Chalcolithic farming culture of Romania, Moldova and Ukraine, which built the largest settlements in the prehistoric world.

name: Trypillia Mega-Sites
summary: Settlements of up to 320 hectares and perhaps 15,000 people, laid out in concentric rings with no palace, citadel or centre.

name: The Drowning of Doggerland
summary: The slow submergence of the land connecting Britain to the continent, which displaced Mesolithic populations and finally made Britain an island.

name: Ertebolle Culture
summary: Complex coastal foragers of southern Scandinavia who made pottery, built shell middens, and kept farming at arm's length for centuries.

name: Franchthi Cave
summary: A cave in the Argolid occupied continuously from the Upper Palaeolithic to the end of the Neolithic — and an argument that farming reached Greece by sea.

name: Funnelbeaker Culture
summary: The farming culture of north-central Europe that built the megalithic tombs, and the last before Corded Ware.

name: Kongemose Culture
summary: The middle Mesolithic of southern Scandinavia, between the Maglemosian and the Ertebolle, turning increasingly to the coast.

name: Lascaux Cave Art
summary: This French cave's famous animal paintings were made during a short Upper Paleolithic occupation.

name: Linear Pottery Culture (LBK)
summary: Europe's first farmers built long timber houses and made band-decorated pottery across a wide central-European belt.

name: Lepenski Vir
summary: A Danube Gorges site of trapezoidal houses and carved boulder sculptures, occupied across the transition to farming.

name: Maglemosian
summary: The founding culture of the northern European Mesolithic, working bone and antler in the forests and wetlands left by the retreating ice.

name: Atlantic Megalithic Tradition
summary: Communities built large stone tombs and monuments along Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts.

name: Michelsberg Culture
summary: Causewayed enclosures and flint mines across the Rhineland, the Paris Basin and the Low Countries.

name: The Muge Shell Middens
summary: Enormous mounds of estuarine shell in the Tagus and Sado valleys, used as both settlement and cemetery by foragers who overlapped with the first farmers.

name: Neanderthal Europe
summary: Neanderthals lived across Europe for hundreds of thousands of years before disappearing after a period of overlap with modern humans.

name: Ness of Brodgar
summary: A monumental Orkney complex between two stone circles, with buildings larger than anything else known in Neolithic northwest Europe.

name: Newgrange
summary: An Irish passage tomb built to admit the winter solstice sunrise, older than Stonehenge's standing stones and older than the pyramids.

name: The Obanian
summary: Shell middens around Oban and on Oronsay, Scotland's main evidence that late foragers there lived substantially off the sea.

name: Ötzi
summary: The naturally preserved body of a man who died in the Alps gives a close view of Copper Age life.

name: Sauveterrian
summary: A narrow-blade microlithic tradition of France, Italy and Iberia, the southern counterpart to the Maglemosian.

name: Sesklo
summary: A Thessalian tell settlement, type-site for the Greek Neolithic sequence and among the earliest farming villages in Europe.

name: Skara Brae
summary: The best-preserved Neolithic village in Europe, its stone furniture still standing in the houses.

name: Star Carr
summary: A waterlogged Yorkshire site preserving the earliest known built structures in Britain, along with antler headdresses.

name: Starcevo-Koros-Cris
summary: The founding Neolithic complex of the Balkans and Carpathian Basin, ancestral to both the Linear Pottery Culture and Vinca.

name: Stonehenge Construction
summary: Stonehenge was built and changed in several stages over roughly fifteen centuries.

name: Varna Necropolis
summary: A Black Sea cemetery holding the oldest worked gold known anywhere, and the earliest clear evidence of concentrated wealth in Europe.

name: Vinca Culture
summary: The major Late Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, with large tell settlements and some of Europe's earliest copper metallurgy.

name: Italian Renaissance
summary: Florentine, Venetian, and Roman flowering; Petrarch, Dante, Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael.

name: Northern Renaissance
summary: Renaissance north of the Alps: Erasmus, Dürer, van Eyck, printing revolution.

name: Plantagenet England
under: England (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe
summary: Three centuries covering Magna Carta, the first English parliaments, the Black Death, the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of the Roses.

name: Stuart England / Britain
under: England (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe
summary: Union of the English and Scottish crowns, civil war, regicide, republic, restoration and the constitutional settlement of 1688.

name: Capetian France
under: France (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe

name: Napoleonic Era
under: France (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe
summary: Napoleon Bonaparte's dominance of Europe from consul to emperor and exile.

name: French Revolution
under: France (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe
summary: Overthrew the Bourbon monarchy and reshaped modern politics.

name: Valois France
under: France (Medieval to Modern) < Western Europe < Europe

name: Andes
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Potato, llama, alpaca and guinea pig, domesticated in the high basin around Lake Titicaca.

name: Eastern North America
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Squash, sunflower, marsh elder and chenopod — a fully independent centre, and one of the latest.

name: Fertile Crescent
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Wheat, barley, lentil, pea, sheep, goat, pig and cattle — the package that reached Europe, North Africa and South Asia.

name: Mesoamerica
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Squash first, then maize and beans — the squash predates maize by over four thousand years.

name: New Guinea Highlands
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Taro and banana, cultivated at Kuk Swamp entirely independently of Asia.

name: Southwest Amazonia
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Manioc and squash cultivated on forest islands of the Llanos de Moxos, far earlier than Amazonian agriculture was thought to begin.

name: Yangtze Valley
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Rice, domesticated over roughly six millennia from Shangshan to Liangzhu.

name: Yellow River Basin
under: Neolithic Transition < Neolithic < Human Prehistory < Global & Multi-Regional
summary: Broomcorn and foxtail millet, the dryland counterpart to the Yangtze's rice.

name: Acheulean Industry
summary: The handaxe tradition: teardrop-shaped tools worked on both faces, made for well over a million years.

name: Aterian Industry
summary: A North African tradition marked by tanged points, made by early modern humans across the Sahara.

name: Aurignacian Industry
summary: The first widespread modern-human tradition in Europe, associated with the earliest cave art and figurines.

name: Châtelperronian Industry
summary: A short-lived western European tradition made during the overlap between Neanderthals and modern humans.

name: Gravettian Industry
summary: The tradition of the Venus figurines and mammoth-bone dwellings, spanning Europe through the coldest part of the Ice Age.

name: Howiesons Poort Industry
summary: A South African tradition of small backed blades, hafted as composite tools, lasting only a few thousand years.

name: Later Stone Age
summary: The sub-Saharan African tradition of small composite tools that continues into the historical period.

name: Lomekwian Industry
summary: The oldest known stone toolkit: large, heavy cores and flakes struck with techniques unlike the later Oldowan.

name: Magdalenian Industry
summary: The late Ice Age tradition of Lascaux and Altamira, ending as the glaciers retreated.

name: Middle Stone Age
summary: The long African toolmaking tradition during which our own species appeared, and with it pigment, beads and engraving.

name: Monte Verde II
summary: A settlement in southern Chile whose age broke the Clovis-first model of the peopling of the Americas.

name: Mousterian Industry
summary: The flake-tool tradition associated mainly with Neanderthals across Europe and western Asia.

name: Oldowan Industry
summary: The earliest widely recognised stone tools: sharp flakes struck from pebble cores.

name: Solutrean Industry
summary: An Iberian and French tradition known for slender, finely pressure-flaked laurel-leaf points.

name: Still Bay Industry
summary: A brief South African tradition of finely worked leaf-shaped points, an early flowering of complex technique.

name: Lake Mungo
summary: The Willandra Lakes locality of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, two of Australia's oldest known human burials.

name: Madjedbebe
summary: A rock shelter on Mirarr Country in Arnhem Land with very early stone tools and other evidence of occupation.

name: Sahul
summary: The ice-age landmass that joined Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea when sea levels were lower.

name: Bismarck Obsidian Network
summary: Obsidian moved 600 km between islands of the Bismarck Archipelago for some seventeen thousand years — among the longest-running exchange networks known.

name: Torres Strait Settlement
summary: The island chain between New Guinea and Australia, settled at very different times at its two ends.

name: Harappan Deurbanisation
summary: The cities are abandoned over roughly three centuries as the monsoon weakens and inundation agriculture stops paying.

name: Dholavira
summary: A city in a desert with no perennial water, which survived on sixteen reservoirs covering a fifth of its walled area.

name: The Ghaggar-Hakra Question
summary: Whether a great river dried and took the cities with it. The geology says the big glacier-fed river was already gone long before the cities existed.

name: Harappa
summary: The type site, and the best-dated one: a continuous sequence from the Ravi phase to Cemetery H, excavated 1986-1996.

name: Kot Dijian Phase
summary: The Early Harappan phase in which the first city walls, the first writing and the first standardised crafts appear, before the mature cities.

name: Late Harappan Phase
summary: The post-urban centuries. The cities empty and the standardised material culture dissolves into regional styles, but settlement does not stop.

name: Lothal
summary: A small Gujarat settlement with a large baked-brick basin that has been argued over for sixty years: dockyard, or reservoir?

name: Mature Harappan Phase
summary: The urban centuries: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa at full extent, with standardised weights, fired-brick drainage and long-distance trade.

name: Mohenjo-daro
summary: The largest mature Harappan city, with the Great Bath, the citadel mound and a fired-brick drainage system running the length of its streets.

name: Rakhigarhi
summary: The largest Harappan site by area, and the source of the only ancient genome yet recovered from within the civilisation.

name: The Indus Script
summary: Undeciphered, and still argued over at a more basic level: whether the signs encode language at all.

name: Peshwa Era
summary: Peshwas (chief ministers) became the effective rulers; the Maratha confederacy dominated most of India.

name: Bhirrana
summary: A Haryana settlement with a disputed claim to extraordinarily early South Asian occupation.

name: Burzahom
summary: A Kashmir valley site of pit dwellings cut into loess, with a Neolithic sequence running into a megalithic phase.

name: Lahuradewa
summary: A lake-margin site in the middle Ganges plain with very early rice evidence and a long environmental sequence.

name: Mehrgarh
summary: A key early farming settlement in the Indus borderlands whose oldest phase has been radically re-dated.

name: Early Harappan Ravi Phase
summary: The earliest well-dated phase at Harappa, before the later urban Indus city.

name: The Ashmounds
summary: Mounds of burnt cattle dung, some many metres high, built up by repeated firing of cattle pens over less than two centuries.

name: South Indian Millet Domestication
summary: Browntop and foxtail millet with mung bean and horsegram, argued to be domesticated in peninsular India rather than introduced.

name: Arrival of Steppe Ancestry in South Asia
summary: The window in which steppe pastoralist ancestry entered South Asia, after the Harappan cities had already emptied.

name: Later Vedic
summary: Eastward settlement into the Ganges plain, iron, larger polities, and the Brahmanas and early Upanishads.

name: Early Vedic (Rigvedic)
summary: The period of the Rigveda: pastoral, mobile, and in the northwest.

name: Ming Occupation
under: Vietnam (dynastic) < Mainland Southeast Asia < Southeast Asia
summary: Administered by the Ming as the province of Jiaozhi, not as a Vietnamese state at all.

name: Nguyễn Lords (Đàng Trong)
under: Later Lê Dynasty < Vietnam (dynastic) < Mainland Southeast Asia < Southeast Asia
summary: Ruled the south independently in practice, expanding into the Mekong delta at Cham and Khmer expense.

name: Trịnh Lords (Đàng Ngoài)
under: Later Lê Dynasty < Vietnam (dynastic) < Mainland Southeast Asia < Southeast Asia
summary: Ruled the north in the Lê emperor's name, holding real power for two and a half centuries.

name: Dabenkeng Culture
under: The Austronesian Expansion < Southeast Asian Prehistory < Southeast Asia
summary: Taiwan's founding Neolithic, with cord-marked pottery, polished stone and millet — the archaeological anchor of the Austronesian homeland.

name: Settlement of the Marianas
under: The Austronesian Expansion < Southeast Asian Prehistory < Southeast Asia
summary: The first crossing into Remote Oceania — some 2,000 km of open ocean, the longest voyage anyone had yet made.

name: Ban Chiang
summary: A northeast Thai burial site central to the re-dating of Southeast Asian bronze metallurgy.

name: Ban Non Wat
summary: The Thai site whose 75 modelled radiocarbon dates rebuilt the chronology of Southeast Asian prehistory.

name: Da But Culture
summary: Shell-midden communities in northern Vietnam with basket-marked pottery, conventionally marking the end of the Hoabinhian way of life.

name: Hoabinhian
summary: A long-lived cave and rockshelter tool tradition of mainland Southeast Asia, often identified by worked pebble tools.

name: Khok Phanom Di
summary: An estuarine mound on the Gulf of Siam with a seven-stage mortuary sequence built up in only five centuries.

name: Man Bac
summary: A northern Vietnamese cemetery whose 85 burials hold both resident foragers and incoming farmers, side by side.

name: Niah Caves Deep Skull
summary: A human skull from Borneo's Niah Caves, now accepted as Late Pleistocene rather than a later burial.

name: Non Nok Tha
summary: With Ban Chiang, one of the two sites behind the claim that Southeast Asia invented bronze first — and behind its collapse.

name: Toalean Culture
summary: A hunter-gatherer tradition confined to a corner of South Sulawesi, which outlasted the arrival of farming around it by millennia.

name: Yangtze Rice Domestication
summary: A gradual process in the lower Yangtze in which managed wild rice became fully domesticated rice.

name: Hattusa
summary: The Hittite capital, source of the royal archives, and — contrary to the story everyone tells — probably not sacked.

name: Troy
summary: Nine cities stacked on one mound at Hisarlik, one of which may or may not be Homer's.

name: Domestication of the Dromedary
summary: The pack animal that made the incense route possible, domesticated far later than the trade routes it is usually credited with opening.

name: The Marib Dam
under: Saba < Pre-Islamic Arabia < Arabia < West Asia
summary: Sabaean hydraulic engineering on a scale that watered a desert kingdom, and whose failure became a parable.

name: Umm an-Nar Culture
summary: The Oman peninsula's Bronze Age of circular stone tower tombs, copper export, and carnelian carried in from the Indus.

name: Wadi Suq Period
summary: The southeastern Arabian second millennium, when the tower-tomb tradition breaks and burial practice changes shape.

name: Linear Elamite
summary: A later Iranian script, claimed in 2022 to have been deciphered as the oldest purely phonographic writing known.

name: Chogha Zanbil
under: Middle Elamite Period < Elam < Iran < West Asia
summary: A royal city built around the best-preserved ziggurat in Iran, abandoned unfinished with thousands of unused bricks still on site.

name: Proto-Elamite
summary: Southwestern Iran's own writing system, invented within a century or two of Mesopotamia's and still undeciphered.

name: Susa
summary: Occupied for six thousand years, capital of Elam, and the place the Code of Hammurabi was found — because the Elamites took it there.

name: Under Assyria
under: Phoenician City-States < Mesopotamia & Levant < West Asia
summary: Tributary to Assyria, with the cities retaining their kings.

name: Under Babylon
under: Phoenician City-States < Mesopotamia & Levant < West Asia
summary: Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Tyre for thirteen years.

name: Late Bronze Age Canaanite Phase
under: Phoenician City-States < Mesopotamia & Levant < West Asia
summary: The cities under Egyptian and Hittite overlordship, before the collapse that freed them.

name: Phoenician Independence
under: Phoenician City-States < Mesopotamia & Levant < West Asia
summary: Three centuries of genuine autonomy after the Bronze Age Collapse removed the empires above them — the period of the alphabet and the western voyages.

name: Under Persia
under: Phoenician City-States < Mesopotamia & Levant < West Asia
summary: Achaemenid subjects supplying the imperial navy, still ruled by their own kings — which is why 539 is the wrong place to end Phoenicia.

name: 'Ain Ghazal
summary: A large Jordanian village of the pre-pottery Neolithic, known for lime plaster statues among the oldest large human figures ever made.

name: Çatalhöyük
summary: A densely packed Anatolian town of mud-brick houses entered through the roof, with wall paintings and burials beneath the floors.

name: Geometric Kebaran
under: Epipalaeolithic (Levant) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: The Middle Epipalaeolithic, named for its geometric microliths, between the Kebaran and the Natufian.

name: Kebaran
under: Epipalaeolithic (Levant) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: The Early Epipalaeolithic of the Levant: small mobile groups with microlithic toolkits, through the Last Glacial Maximum.

name: Göbekli Tepe
summary: Monumental enclosures raised by people who were not yet farming, in southeastern Anatolia.

name: Halaf Culture
summary: Northern Mesopotamian villages known for finely painted polychrome pottery traded over long distances.

name: Neolithic Jericho
summary: The oldest known town wall and stone tower, built by people who farmed but had not yet made pottery.

name: Jemdet Nasr Period
under: Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: The short period between Uruk and the Early Dynastic, in which writing spreads beyond Uruk and becomes recognisably cuneiform.

name: Proto-Cuneiform
under: Uruk Period < Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: The earliest known writing: numerals and word-signs pressed into clay at Uruk, used almost entirely for accounting.

name: Uruk
under: Uruk Period < Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: The first city: about 100 hectares by the end of the period, holding more than half the settled area of southern Mesopotamia around it.

name: The Uruk Expansion
under: Uruk Period < Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia) < West Asian Prehistory < West Asia
summary: Uruk material culture appears across Syria and into Anatolia, and scholars have argued for forty years about what that means.

name: Natufian Culture
summary: Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who settled in one place, built stone houses and buried their dead with ornaments, before anyone farmed.

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
summary: The first farming villages, before pottery: round houses, stored grain and communal building.

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B
summary: Rectangular houses, plastered skulls and the first fully domesticated herds of sheep and goats.

name: Ubaid Period
summary: The long southern Mesopotamian prelude to cities: irrigation, temples on platforms, and the settlement pattern Sumer inherits.
